And then at para 116 at page 43, you explain that further noting there was a noticeable absence of the pupae of blowflies among the bodies, and explained that one might expect to find those if the bodies had been exposed for days in high season when blowflies were active. And I take it that was, as seems to be indicated in paragraph 103, another indication of the length of time that might have transpired between the placement of bodies in the grave and their covering?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, there was a lack of blowfly pupae observed during the excavation. Depending on time of year, flies would lay eggs quite rapidly, and it's common in excavations where bodies that have been supposed for sometime before burial to find these pupae. None were observed during the excavation that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The second entomological factor is found at paragraph 116 at page 43 and is associated with Figure 37, and that's the identification of a beetle, which you indicate is the Necrodes Littoralis. And can you quickly explain to the Court the significance of the finding of that beetle in the grave?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. These beetles were observed. It was not known what they were. They were found between compressed bodies. On contacting colleagues, experts at the Natural History Museum in London, they identified from a photograph the species and indicated that to me and indicated it's a species active between a certain time of year between -- normally between April and October. They were found within blankets in between bodies which is in -- consistent with them having come to the grave with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that the information about those beetles is that they don't burrow into the ground?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, that information was also provided to me by the Natural History Museum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So further limiting the period of time when they would have entered the grave to the -- and the manner in which they would have entered the grave; correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Tieger, you earlier referred to paragraph 103, page 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is obviously incorrect because 103 is on page 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you what to look for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And I'll check the reference to -- I presume the paragraph identification was the correct identifier, but I'll double-check the reference to make sure it wasn't meant to be, for some reason, something on page 35, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find the flies on page -- in paragraph 103, and I fail to find them there. Witness, could you assist where you deal with the entomological -- the first entomological issue that Mr. Tieger raised; that is, the presence of pupae of that fly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I might be able to assist, Mr. President. It does turn out that page 35 is correct, but it's paragraph 106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 106. Yes, Witness, you said -- in this context you said that this -- you would expect, depending on the season, you would expect the pupae of this blowfly to be present if the bodies would have been exposed for a longer period of time to open air.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what seasons would you expect them, what seasons would you not expect them or to expect them to appear later, if it is within your expertise? Because I noticed that you mainly reproduced what others told you. If you're confident to tell us something about it, please do so, but then also explain to us why you consider yourself in a position to answer that question, and if not please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. No, I'm not an entomologist. I do not have entomological expertise but observe in graves the evidence encountered, and it's frequently observed that -- to find blowfly pupae when bodies have been interred in the spring through to autumn season when temperatures are higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you refraining from any expert opinion about that but that's what you observed in the past, that such pupae were found in that season of the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- Mr. Lukic, I hardly dare to ask you whether you're ready to cross-examine the witness but.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would say I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, yes, that's the reason why I didn't ask you in view of the recent developments. Mr. Lukic, you have an opportunity now to cross-examine the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hanson, Mr. Lukic is standing to your left, he's counsel for Mr. Mladic, and he may have questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will not from the problem with the overlapping since I will pose my questions in B/C/S, so you don't have to be mindful of any pauses. [Interpretation] In your report on page 5, you stated all the people who were present including Mr. Paul Grady, an investigator of this Tribunal. Could you please tell us what Mr. Grady's role was?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I understand he was liaising with the prosecutor's office about the investigation of the Tomasica site.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you have any contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, he was present during the excavation when the discussion was ongoing about what was being found and how to undertake the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you get any tasks from Mr. Grady?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Tasks from Mr. Grady? No. My co-ordination on what to undertake at the site was undertaken in co-ordination with the prosecutor's office and missing persons institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So who issued the tasks from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: The representative of the prosecutor's office who was there on a day-to-day basis Eldar Jahic, so the discussion on how to proceed with the excavation was had between him, the missing persons institute staff, and myself, or my ICMP staff if I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you worked for the prosecutor's office of the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina and not for the Prosecutor's Office for this Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was called, and ICMP was called to assist and provide technical advice by the Bosnian prosecutor's Office, state prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will come to your co-operation with the missing persons institute in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you aware that according to Mr. Karahasanovic's work, it was established that some evidence from the field arrived in bags that were not closed?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: From the field, you mean the Tomasica excavation site?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: To which location? You said bags arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the location where Mrs. Karahasanovic worked.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Karahasanovic. Who is she, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you don't know, that's -- I'll move. [Interpretation] Are you aware that artefacts from the field were sent for examination in open bags?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had that been the case, would that mean that protocols on work in the field were not adhered to?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I understand the chain of custody of all the evidence was undertaken by the crime technicians in Prijedor police, so I couldn't really comment on what happened to the evidence once it was under their custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat my question. Would the fact that the artefacts from the field arrived for examination in open bags mean that protocols about the work in the field were not adhered to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The problem with that question is the one identified by the witness, that there's a gap between the two. And the witness -- and the question ignores that. So there's one issue about what the protocol in the field were, there's another issue about what the conditions of the bags may have been when they arrived at a place that the witness is unfamiliar with, and he tried to indicate that what transpired in between in connection with organisations that are not identified for his benefit that he can't comment on. I think in those circumstances, it's not exactly a fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is of a more general nature, whether that would -- that would be in contradiction with protocols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now you are phrasing the question in a more general way, protocols. Earlier you said protocols on work in the field, whereas you then said something about when they arrived. If you would please explore that in detail, what protocols applied for this witness and whether he has any knowledge of protocols that may have applied to subsequent stages of the investigation, and whether he would then consider such a thing to happen to be in violation of either the protocol in the field or any other protocol he is aware of. If you would explore it in that way, then I think we would get to the information you are seeking and at the same time it would -- Mr. Tieger, it would meet your concerns, if I understood them well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, there's -- that sounds like a procedure that will work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed that way in a very precise manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hanson, the protocols that you adhered to, do they assume that artefacts that are to be sent for examination are packed and closed?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: On the Tomasica site, ICMP and myself were not in control of chain of custody or handling of evidence once it came from the grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question. Yeah, you say the protocols you adhere to. Now, did the protocols which applied on from finding artefacts up to leaving your custody, did they say anything about them to be put in closed bags or in a closed container?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The site removal of evidence from the grave was undertaken by crime technicians helped -- with the bodies helped by ICMP staff. The procedure the crime technicians took to handle the evidence and package it were not part of what ICMP did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, irrespective of whether ICMP did it, if you would have done it, would there have been certain protocols to put them in bags and to close those bags?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The standard procedure for handling evidence in chain of custody is to make sure it is properly packaged, labelled, and sealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's just a first step but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps you could ask, Mr. Lukic, whether the witness observed what was done by those who were not bound by these protocols, but -- so that we have a factual basis for any follow-up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the technicians were in charge of the bags and the packing of the artefacts. Who were they supervised by?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I understand an inspector from the Prijedor police, the prosecutor's office representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "representatives of the prosecutor's office," you mean the prosecutor's office of the state court in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that a number of graves were opened at the same time?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the recommendation of the commission from San Antonio not uncover more than one grave at the same time?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: San Antonio Commission? No, I don't think I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you did not follow the instructions of the San Antonio Commission because were not aware of the commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: As you describe it, the San Antonio Commission, no, I do not know to which you refer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, is it because Mr. Lukic is not precisely enough describing such a commission, or have you ever heard about a commission which was referred to or linked to by whomever with San Antonio, or do you say San Antonio Commission doesn't ring a bell at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour. It doesn't ring a bell with me, San Antonio Commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hanson, how long did you work on this particular case, the Tomasica case?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: In the field or overall?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] In total, yeah.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: In the field?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In total.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Ongoing from the 6th of September through to April 2014, and then with report-writing, then into May 2014.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can assume that September was 2013.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: September 2013, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 4 of your report, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could I ask one follow-up question. Witness, questions were asked about the packaging of artefacts, whatever was found. Did you ever observe that artefacts found were not packed in -- in a way as you would have done it? So I'm not asking you as an expert now but just on whether you observed any of such thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of your report, you say that 371 cases of human remains were recovered.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us exactly what that is, what the 370 cases of human remains was?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: That includes all bodies, body parts, and cases of -- known as general bones. That's loose bones collected from the main grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this last category, does that have anything to do with the cases that you discussed and that you were asked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And these cases, are they connected to any names or do they just have numbers?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: At the time of collection, they're given evidence numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then later, they were connected to the bodies, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Each body or body part or piece of evidence identified is provided with an evidence -- a sequential evidence number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the exhumations, was it the case that some bones were left over that were not connected to any particular body?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Within the graves and within the mixed brown soil, loose bones and fragments of bones were found, and they were collected within these cases designated GB.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] GB, you mean general bags?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: General bags, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later, each one of those loose bones that were not associated with a body, was it given a number?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Do you mean at the excavation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] At the end of the process.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I do not know. So what happened to the general cases and how they were dealt with, the general bones case, how they're dealt with in examination, I do not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. [Interpretation] I'm just going to have one more question in this connection. Do you know anything about the final list of names of missing persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: The final list of persons missing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You mean a national list, sir? Or related to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] On a national level.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: On a national level, I know there is a list undergoing verification, a CEN list. Other than that, I do not have any involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we look at a Figure 41, please. You spoke about that several times today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to locate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 46, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 46. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This illustration, this figure, could you please tell us how much of the Tomasica grave was actually robbed or disturbed?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: In volume, I would say 30 to 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back to paragraph 8 now; page 2. There, you say: "A thick deposit of mixed brown clay was excavated from which 17 cases of remains were recovered."

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of cases of remains are they? Which parts of body?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be page 7 and not 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is page 7. I stand corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These cases from the mixed brown clay were bodies, body parts, and cases of general bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain the minimum number of bodies there may have been?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: From the mixed brown clay? We were not. We passed the cases for examination at the mortuaries to determine those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, they were supposed to do the matching between the remains referred to here and other sets of remains or complete bodies.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people working at the location, were they also supervised by you?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: The ICMP staff? Yes, they were. And in my absence, by a deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek clarification. Mr. Lukic, you asked whether the matching would be done between the remains referred to here and other sets of remains or complete bodies, and the witness says: "That's correct." But have you excluded on purpose the matching within that set of cases which --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By omission. I could say by omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By omission. May I take it that that would be a possible matching exercise as well, that certain cases within that group of 17 would have given a match?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I have a follow-up question. If it's a piece -- is matched with a complete body, it can't be a part of that body, could it? Because the body is complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My understanding that still complete body can miss a bone or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then it's not complete if it misses a bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I'm not an expert. Maybe the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, there's a problem with your question. If a body is complete, it misses nothing; therefore, there's no point in comparing it to anything else. So that question doesn't make sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would try to clarify with the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hanson, you heard doubts Honourable Judge Moloto has. Can you explain and enlighten us on this issue, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. A case may be designated a body but it may not be complete, so it may be missing a lower part of a leg, for example, it may be missing a hand, so it gets the case designation of body. If a lower leg is found that is then matched through DNA and other techniques, it's reassociated to that body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Based on my understanding of your definition of case a little earlier, then it becomes impossible or it cannot happen that a case is a body? Because as I understand you, if I'm correct, a case is a part of a body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A case can be a body, it can be a body part; that is, a lower leg. It could be one bone. A case is what is found as one distinct set of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that would include a complete body that doesn't miss anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- some of these bodies which have soft tissue are complete, there's nothing missing from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then I have a better understanding of what you mean by "case."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It we look at paragraph 17, which is on the next page, for clarification, and for the purposes of the record, you say there that: "Entomological evidence indicates the last bodies may have been put into the graves between April and October." What year?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: We do not know which year. The evidence from the excavation provided a chronology and sequence of events but no finite dating by year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 20, you explain that the bodies were examined and recorded and transported to Krajina Identification Project, KIP, at Sejkovaca mortuary. Sejkovaca is in Sanski Most, which is the Federation; correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that a well-equipped mortuary?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: By common standards, I would say it's not a well-equipped mortuary, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who elected that mortuary and not, for example, the one in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 25, which is on the next page, you state -- [In English] actually, two pages ahead. Okay. Next page in B/C/S. [Interpretation] You say: "According to the information provided to ICMP in 2006, the Tomasica mine complex site was believed to have originally contained 100 to 200 individuals who died on or around the 20th of July 1992 in the Brdo area. There was further information that persons who died at the Keraterm camp around the 24th of July 1992 were also buried at the site." Did the work carried out by you confirm any of this, or is this that you simply present as information you learned from someone else?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, that information was present in the report, ICMP excavation report from 2006. The excavation 2013, which I report upon in my report, provided no information that I know of about bodies from the Brdo area or Keraterm camp, the excavation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should not speak aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is, perhaps can I clarify. What I mean is that I gathered no information during the excavation related to origin of the bodies found within the graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's because you didn't identify them by name or by person? That was not part of your task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not part of my task, Your Honour, during excavation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, did you not double-check this piece of information provided by the institute for missing persons to ICMP about the possibility of 8- to 900 bodies that may have been brought to the site between May and July 1992?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: This background information is coming from the reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should not speak aloud. And that's now the second time, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if I may give you, Mr. Lukic, as guidance, that if a report, which one would expect to clearly state if some identification or if some verification would have been done, if it's not in the report, this Chamber, as a starting point, will take it that such verification has not taken place. Especially here. It's just reported as this is information. And if there would have been a verification, I take it that the witness would have mentioned that in his report. This is -- may save some time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But still I deemed it necessary to clarify with the witness. Since we have it in the report. I have to check whether it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. If the report says Mr. A told me that he bought a red car yesterday, and if there's nothing else in it, then the Chamber will take it that that is what that witness heard and that he has not verified neither the colour neither the day of -- well, if you would have to check everything or if you have to -- what is not in the report, if you would have to seek verification that what is not the report didn't take place, unless there's any specific reason to believe, but your questions in relation to paragraph 25, reading the report as a whole, make it clear that it was not within the task of this witness to verify that. And if he would have done so, it may be -- it -- one would not expect it not to appear in the report, and if it's not in the report, it's not there for us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution whose witness testified -- testifies for them had necessity to clarify some things, so I think that we are on -- entitled to clarify certain things from the report as well, especially -- I was not clear. If this was maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gave you the guidance how this Chamber operates, Mr. Lukic, and then use your time as you wish. But if there are more important matters to be dealt with, then that might be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 28, Mr. Hanson, you state that: "Between the 14th of June and 30th of June 2006 the excavation continued at the same location ..." You also state that the Una-Sana cantonal police crime technicians took custody of all evidence. Perhaps a matter of clarification. The Una-Sana cantonal police is part of the Federation police force; correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the answer to that. But, again, this paragraph is quoting from the 2007 report that I used for reference in this background section.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, my question is: Who decided that evidence was to be kept in the Federation, which is to say outside of Republika Srpska where it had originally been found?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, sir. The contents of this paragraph are in reference to the 2007 report I am quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 30, you say that additionally the Jakarina Kosa secondary grave had been excavated in 2001 under the auspices of the ICTY and that a total of 139 bodies and 259 body parts were recovered, and the MNI of 298 was established based on anthropological examination. Did you have any participation in this exercise or does it also come from the 2006 report?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I did not participate in that, sir. The information is from the published article of 2006 by Baraybar and Gasior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the sentences following, you say: "Subsequent DNA matching demonstrated linkages between cases from the Jakarina Kosa and Tomasica graves. Identifications have been made for cases recovered from Tomasica and Jakarina Kosa by MPI based on ICMP DNA match reports." What was the role of the ICMP in this process, and did you play a role?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: No, I did not play a role in any of the DNA identification. ICMP supports the MPI Bosnia authorities in undertaking identifications using its DNA laboratory facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is the laboratory located?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: ICMP's facilities are based in Sarajevo, Tuzla, and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the analyses were conducted?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: From these cases from 2001, no, sir, I couldn't inform you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] And 2006?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: No, that -- I wasn't involved in 2006 excavation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know whether in 2001 and 2006 the ICMP laboratories for DNA analysis possessed the required certifications?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: You would have to address that, I think, to my colleagues within ICMP who have their expertise in DNA and laboratories.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. We'll do so. Thank you, sir. [Interpretation] May we conclude, then, that you do not know what made the laboratories conclude on the figures and what procedures they used?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Which figures, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 139 bodies and 298 parts of bodies and the MNI of 298.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Undertaken by anthropological examination? No, I was not involved in those examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see in several instances in your report that there is information which you had not worked on and you are unable to explain. Why did you then include such information in your report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you please clearly state where the witness does so so that the Chamber also can check in the context whether there could be any doubt as to whether the witness - because that's the issue - is apparently leading information, hiding that it is information that he just got from others or where -- could you please be specific in that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I said that he -- this gentleman was hiding anything, but I did ask him, for example, let's say paragraph 30, why is this included in his report. Obviously he has no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's, indeed, what you're suggesting, that there's no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please be specific. I withdraw whether it's misleading or not. But at least mixing up information he has gained himself with information he received from others and why that's done, could you be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Can it be gleaned from your report what are the matters you personally were involved in as opposed to parts of the work carried out that you were not involved in?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. The paragraph you've referred to in the background section. It's standard in our reports to provide a background which is the information already available before the undertaking of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. That clarifies the issue, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. If it would be a suitable moment for a break --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we'll take that break now. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 30 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hanson, do you know who Milutin Misic is?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you said that you contacted members of the institute for missing persons of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did your contacts go through him or through Mr. Amor Masovic? Regarding the work on Tomasica, when you talk about paragraph 31, for example.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: The initial discussion which included discussion about the Tomasica site was undertaken and arranged through Dusan Pavlovic, who's the exhumations department head at MPI. In December 2012, we had a general meeting with staff from MPI offices all across Bosnia to discuss ways to better the search for finding graves, and it was the field officers from the MPI Bihac office who raised at that general meeting the Tomasica site and whether there was potentially more work to do there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, paragraph 31, you say that deep trenching by MPI and the prosecutor's office staff was conducted on the 4th to 5th September of 2013. Do you know how the staff from the MPI and the prosecutor's office carried out this trenching?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: No, I was not present on those dates. I'd received a phone call from Eldar Jahic stating they'd undertaken trenching and had uncovered human remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you kindly repeat the name because it was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Eldar Jahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Is it correctly spelled on your screen? Can you check it?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: My screen is blank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's the second name on page 5 of the report, sir. You can find it there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that corresponds to the spelling in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Did you write this report?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you able to explain to us why at the end of the paragraph your name is mentioned in the third person singular?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's simply a self-description.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand. Did you refer to yourself in this way throughout the report or not?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: No, I believe that's the only instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 42 of your report, can we look at that, please. When we're talking about the method and the archaeological excavation of the grave and other structures, you say that the excavation process was overseen by the deputy director of the forensic sciences for archaeology and anthropology at ICMP, supported by ICMP archaeologists. Are you able to give us the names of these persons?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I am deputy director for forensic sciences for archaeology and anthropology, and the names of the archaeologists are listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right. I was just interested in this very first point. Again, we have the third person singular. So I was confused as to whether you wrote the entire report or only just sections of it.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: No, I wrote the entire report, and where necessary I described my own title and name. For clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at paragraph 71 now. [In English] In B/C/S, it's page 24. Should be page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the -- this paragraph, it states --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is not the right paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the interpreters initially had some problems, I think, with the paragraph. Is it clear now? Could you then repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 71. Yes. Could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The properties of each case were recorded on body forms to aid the pathologists and mortuary team during later examinations. All remains were transported to the Sejkovaca mortuary in Sanski Most under the direction of the court pathologist."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that our numbering of paragraphs does not correspond to what Mr. Lukic has read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could have you a look at paragraph 71. Of course, in the B/C/S, I do not know whether it is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do have it on the screen now but not on our hard copy. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it possible that the interpreters were provided with the same wrong hard copy as the Judges were initially and could then instead of printing it out for us could you immediately take care that the interpreters have the right paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Court is correct about that. The interpreters received copies last week. And as it turns out, I guess we printed those out for the benefit of the booth. We'll distribute those now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters' booth will be provided with an accurate copy corresponding with what is now on our screens, both in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can read out paragraph 71 now because we see it on the screen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Any evidence found on a body remained with the body after initial examination so that it could be dealt with during the mortuary examination, unless the prosecutor deemed it necessary to remove it for evidential purposes. Such evidence was not always noted or observed by ICMP staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now your question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us who decided whether it -- what was necessary to be removed from the body? Was that the prosecutor or was it the ICMP staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The answer to that question is in the paragraph 71 that you just read, Mr. Lukic: "... unless the prosecutor deemed it necessary ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't clear, but my question was more who -- who decided and allow the removal. So if the prosecution deems something necessary doesn't mean that he has the power to remove it. Maybe he has to ask somebody. Maybe I wasn't clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's clarify it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your question is on what authority --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Authority, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the prosecutor could decide that it was necessary to remove evidence for evidential purposes from a body. Could you answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On what authority the prosecutor? No, I couldn't answer that question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said in the paragraph that the ICMP staff did not always observe or record such evidence. Do you know who kept the records about the evidence and the chain of custody?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: The crime technicians, I believe, kept the evidence logs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You believe so or you know so?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I believe. I was not present at the excavation every day, but that was the protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And was it customary for the ICMP to be informed about the removal of evidence?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And could we agree that you don't know how the procedure actually went on?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: You mean on a day-to-day basis, how the evidence was dealt with when examined after taking from the grave? No, ICMP wasn't involved with in looking at the cases once they came from the grave and before they went to the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, nevertheless, give us examples of what was, for example, as far -- because you make these observations so you must have some knowledge about incidents where this happened, could you tell us anything about the frequency of such incidents and could you give us one or two examples of what kind of material was separated from the bodily remains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Once the body was put a body bag, put on a stretcher, and carried from the grave, it was placed down. The crime technicians, prosecutor, and MPI then together looked through the body, examine it more closely. They were looking for personal effects and documents, I think, that related potentially to the identifications of the persons. Checks, of course, were also made for safety reasons to make sure there was nothing dangerous upon the bodies such as munitions, because during the excavation we're not certain as we find each body as to its nature and properties. So I think typically that's the type of thing that was undertaken with a recording of documents and any personal effects found on the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your recollection, was this a frequent thing to happen or -- I mean, was it once out of ten or was it quite often that it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was present on site, I think it's quite a frequent thing. Every -- every case was checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at paragraph 79 now, please. It's two pages on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here, you state the following. I quote: "Exposed remains were lifted after recording and surveying by the anthropologists. Some remains designated as general bones and found during excavation in the mixed brown clay were moved for numbering and recording, so that excavation could continue." Let me ask you this first: Who moved these artefacts?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: The general bones?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] All artefacts that were mentioned in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Some of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the word "artefact," would you include bones as artefacts? Because it's my understanding of the English word "artefact" that it's something made by man rather than grown by nature. And therefore, could you please indicate, Mr. Lukic, where in paragraph 79 you find a reference to artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will use English then. Human remains. My understanding might be wrong. I would mark artefact everything, bones and man-made artefacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a native English speaker, but I tried to at least to explain how I understand the word "artefact," and I didn't hear any objections to that until now, so ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I could easily accept that I'm not an English speaking person either, and I don't have perfect understanding of English words, so, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto confirms that my understanding of the word "artefact" is correct. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we have to abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hanson, these human remains recovered, who would remove them?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: After recording, the anthropologists assisted the mortuary technician staff to put the body in the body bag, and then it was carried from the grave by the mortuary technician staff. If I'd just add to that, the general bones found during the excavation in the mixed brown clay, often these were found after they'd been moved; that is, the heavy machinery clearing the clay would expose bones where they would be observed once they'd been moved onto the spoil heaps, and the mortuary technician staff and the anthropologists were observing that work. In that instance then, those remains were put into a general bag and collected by area because they're in effect toward -- they were already moved and disturbed. And the putting into those general bags, that might be done by the anthropologists. Normally, the mortuary technicians upon finding those remains would call an anthropologist to confirm that they were human remains and that they should be put in a general bag. Those general bags were collected and put with the other body bags and then checked in the normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that anthropologists assist the mortuary technician staff. Those mortuary technician staff were employed by whom?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: The Sanski Most mortuary company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The general bones marked as co-mingled bones as part of remains this remains, is it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic kindly repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does it involve cases as well?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, one -- a general bone case, it is a case of evidence. It may come -- combine a single bone or several bones recovered from the same general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of your work, were you warned against such cases possibly creating problems in determining the number of people who died?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: No, the -- the designation of the general bones body or body part is really to understand how they can be collected as cases of evidence at the site. How many individuals may be represented within the bones within a general bag case is determined in the mortuary. If several bones are found loose in an area, it -- we cannot tell if they're from one individual or multiple individuals. That's -- the examination of that case to determine if it is one or more persons is undertaken in the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As an ICMP employee, did you possibly hear of criticisms involving such cases that make it more difficult to determine the overall number of those who were killed in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: No, it's always difficult because the number of cases recovered in the field is not necessarily representative of the number of individuals determined under examination, simply because in many occasions grave-sites the remains are mixed and the team working in the field does not have the ability to determine how many individuals might be present within the cases recovered. Often remains of more than one individual are recovered in one case because the bones are fragmented or mixed up, and at site you cannot tell which bones necessarily belong to which individual when they are loose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was simply whether you heard of criticisms to that extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that was not your question, Mr. Lukic. Your question was, at least as it was translated to us, whether the witness heard of criticisms involving such cases that make it more difficult to determine the overall number of those who were killed in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... That's a rather wide --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he actually heard criticism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what then followed is pretty incomprehensible, such cases that made it more important. So I think that the witness tried to best of his abilities to answer the question. But if you want it ask the question whether he heard of any criticism about the work done by the ICMP, then the witness may be able to answer that question. Can you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, criticism of ICMP using these designations, no. Within the anthropological community in North America, SWGANTH, which is an anthropological collective which is producing standards of work, I know there is discussion about whether to use these nomenclatures of body, body parts, general bag. That discussion involved the potential to bias examinations, and I know this because the standing operating procedure SWGANTH produced I contributed to, but I know of no criticism that it makes identification or the number of individuals determined more -- more difficult, because the subsequent examination is very detailed and separate from the field collection activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was some mention of paragraph 103 today where you mentioned the moving of bodies. I'm interested in knowing whether bodies were moved only from parts of the grave or were there attempts to move the grave as a whole without the job ever being completed?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I think I understand the question as was the whole of the grave moved or parts it. The evidence is consistent with just a part of the grave being moved within those areas I designated as within the robbing cuts which are within the dotted lines in Figure, I think, 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] 41, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's when also you mentioned some 30 to 40 per cent of it being moved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So this question has been answered already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the part of the question that may not have been answered yet is whether you were able to conclude whether attempts were made to move the grave as a whole. That's -- I don't know whether it's within the realm of your expertise, but did find anything that would give us a clue as to whether the intention went beyond a partly removal of the grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There were areas of the grave which are not disturbed. So the whole was -- there's no evidence that the whole grave is disturbed simply because portions of the grave appear undisturbed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there's no evidence which would shed some light on whether it was ever intended to remove the whole grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not from the evidence we have. A part of the grave disturbed and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this falls within your field of expertise, but I will put the question nonetheless. Please tell us if you are unable to answer. In the course of your work, were you ever able to conclude why only 30 to 40 per cent of the grave was moved? Was there any erosion of the soil, was there effect of water? Why was only a part of the grave moved? Do you have an explanation, based on your position?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, the areas disturbed are quite distinctive. They're very different from the areas that were undisturbed. As to why the rest of the grave was not moved, I can't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. Sorry for bothering you with this kind of question but I had for some other purposes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at paragraph 113 next. It is item 6.3, "Nature and Distribution of Artefacts and Physical Evidence." 6.3.1, "Types of Evidence." You say there: "Several types of physical evidence were recovered from the excavation area both within and without the grave ..." And then you enumerate identity card, documents, watches. You go on to say: "These relationships were recorded by the police, prosecutor, and MPI. Several examples were noted by the ICTY investigator. 35 evidence items of this kind were collected." Who controlled the process?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: The evidence collection process? The prosecutors and the crime-scene technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But not you, for the most part?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: No, no, we did -- ICMP did not control any evidence collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, paragraph 113 was read to you. I have some difficulties in understanding "both within and without the grave," where I would expect both within and outside. Is -- could you assist me in understanding your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. "Without" is outside the grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A reference was made today about entomological evidence dealt with by paragraph 116. We saw the image of a beetle. Did you have any relevant experts in that field as part of your team?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: No, there were no entomologists present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 120. Page 54 in the B/C/S and it should be 52 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 51 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 6.5, "Observations Relevant to Assisting With Identifications." Paragraph 120 reads as follows: "There are a number of circumstances associated with this site and the recovery effort that have the potential to assist with identification." In bullet point 1, you say: "After the initial deposition, the grave was later intentionally disturbed with removal of remains to other locations, with the known location being Jakarina Kosa." Except for Jakarina Kosa, what were the other locations, if you can tell us here today?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: I know of no other locations. What I mean by this sentence is the remains are not present on the Tomasica site.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an answer to my question. Let's look at paragraph 127 next, under the heading: "Conclusion." There, you refer to a main grave. You say that: "An irregular squared shape was excavated. It was 3 metres deep, 18 metres in length, and 10 metres wide, from which 371 cases of human remains were recovered." When is a final determination made in terms of how many people were found?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: How many people found. In the mortuary after examinations and receiving of DNA results and other analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the process is completed after your stage of the work; correct?

utterances.speaker: IAN HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. So we're recovering identifiable -- of course, there is a recognised cases of remains as defined as cases of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's approximately the fourth or the fifth time that this witness, apart from describing it very clearly in his report, explains this to us. Witness, we'll have to adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may now -- but before you leave this courtroom, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, irrespective of whether that is testimony given today or still to be given tomorrow. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we adjourn, there may be two matters. First, I'd like to know whether you're on track as far as time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably I will finish him before than I estimated. I estimated four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you give us an indication then as to how much time you'd still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this moment? Maybe I will be able tomorrow morning because I have to go through all the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean to tell us tomorrow morning in the beginning of the session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'd like to hear that from you. Is there any other matter to be announced?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. Mr. Mladic waived his right to be present tomorrow at the trial, and he signed his waiver, so we just want to inform Your Honours that we will proceed without Mr. Mladic tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll then proceed, Mr. Mladic having waived his right to be present, because he knows that he has the right to be present and to attend Court and has chosen tomorrow not to use that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I see Mr. Mladic nodding in the affirmative behind you. Then we'll receive later that confirmation of the waiver, the written confirmation. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, the 25th of June, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
